q: A spectrometer is a scientific instrument used to separate and measure spectral components of a physical phenomenon.
e: True. Wavelengths then fingerprint the source. A microscope magnifies shape; it does not by itself sort colour this way. A spectrometer separates and measures spectral components, usually with a collimator, a disperser and a telescope.

q: The optical spectrometer consists of light source, collimator, dispersion elements and a microscope.
e: False. An optical spectrometer uses a light source, collimator, dispersing element, and a telescope, not a microscope. The telescope views the spectrum. A microscope is the wrong viewing arm.

q: The collimated beam from a specific light source is dispersed by dispersion element such as prism or grating.
e: True. fs is the frequency the source emits; vs is how fast the source moves through the still medium. Source toward the observer raises pitch; source away lowers it. v without a subscript is the wave speed in the medium.

q: In a spectrophotometer, dispersion element combines light into a single beam which is allowed to fall on the sample to be investigated.
e: False. In a spectrophotometer the dispersing element splits light into wavelengths; it does not combine them into one beam. Each slice then probes the sample. Combining would undo the spectrum.

q: Three of the most common optical spectrometers are spectrophotometers, spectrofluorometers and Raman spectrometers.
e: True. Wavelengths then fingerprint the source. A microscope magnifies shape; it does not by itself sort colour this way. Three of the most common optical spectrometers cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.
